evidence: Read CONTEXT whole, then the draft: “Used together properly, the subconscious can feel safer in giving its response, though that doesn't make the answers any more true.” It appears once in CONTEXT, identical to DRAFT.txt, as the closing sentence of the last paragraph, after “You use the prompt to tell your subconscious what you want in a language it can easily understand.” and “The NLP in Appendix B below can help smooth the prompt's entry and reduce resistance.” Read cold it has no seam: “Used together” still points back at the prompt and the NLP of Appendix B, the caveat still follows the claim it qualifies, and “though” as a conjunction is as casual as his trailing “though” was. Against SOURCE (“Used together properly, the subconscious can feel safer in giving its response. That doesn't make the answers any more true, though.”): every word is his and nothing is added or dropped; the only edits are the full stop becoming “, though” and “That” becoming “that”, with the closing “, though” gone. Both halves of the meaning to keep survive in the same order (feeling safer; that does not make the answers more true), and no claim or fact is added. “that” means the subconscious feeling safer, as “That” did, and now sits in the same sentence as its antecedent, so it is anchored at least as well (C02 ABSENT). The straight apostrophe in “doesn't” matches SOURCE and the paragraph's own “prompt's”. One point I weighed hard, because the guide is full of safety cautions: the caveat moves from a sentence of its own to a closing clause, one grammatical rank down. I do not count that as softening: it is still the last words of the paragraph and of the section, in his plain words (“any more true”), and the paragraph before already warns against acting on answers until calm and checked; what goes is the full stop, not the caution. The writer's card should say the caveat is now a clause. Tell rows: all 33 (T01-T29, C01-C04) checked against the literal draft in context; none is PRESENT. T18 ABSENT: the premise-then-short-flip shape belongs to the source's two sentences, the join removes the short sentence, and the caveat qualifies the premise rather than flipping it. T17 ABSENT: it is a specific caution about this technique's answers in his words, not an aphorism or new principle. T12 ABSENT: a necessary contrast (feeling safe versus being true), nothing matched in form. T15 ABSENT: no word swapped for a rarer one. T14 ABSENT: nothing reordered, no point lost; the join reads as sense, not as a move to beat a detector. T29 ABSENT: it is the paragraph's last sentence, but the caveat is a new consideration, and without the sentence the paragraph never says the answers may be untrue. T28 and T20 ABSENT: it ends on a caution, not uplift, in a plain clause, not a polished closer. T21 ABSENT: two of his points, the second qualifying the first. T11 ABSENT: “though” is his own word moved. No first person, scene, tic word, colon or question. Linter finding 'D9 follows the source order' (1/1 paragraphs, agreement 1.00): accepted. It is an in-place join of his two sentences and the caveat has to come after the claim it qualifies, so the order is fixed by the sense; the flag's own test is met, since the caveat is the thing noticed (T13) and the sentence does not give equal weight to its parts (T09).
